title: I think I broke my game -- Enemy AI Search Behavior
author: MosesSecondofHisName
selftext:
I've been developing my game for about a month, and I think I've hit a wall. To keep it short, I want my enemies to search a cave for a (non-moving) target. Initially, I had pretty basic enemy pathing and the result was that the enemies always went straight to the target. So I broke the pathing up into different states (after watching a video on how AI works in stealth games), but it was still very difficult to get them to actually explore the cave naturally as opposed to either 1. going straight to the target; or 2. wandering aimlessly and eventually freeze indefinitely (which is where I'm at now).

I've been trying lots of different fixes, but they all seem to introduce a new problem without resolving the old one, and I worry it may be beyond my ability (and that of the coding functions of Chat GPT). I'm looking for any resources that might help me see this through.

If it helps, I currently have the search broken into three states:

1. Search--in this state, the enemies wander and look around.
2. Decision--this state triggers anytime they reach an intersection and is the math behind how they choose where to go.
3. Charge--once they "spot" the target, the enemies move in and attack

I'm at a point where I'd be willing to just buy an enemy search algo if it exists. But I'm also open to switching to a more sophisticated coding AI. I guess I'm not sure if this is a very basic problem that I can solve with a bit of knowledge or a really complex problem that would take a long time or years of knowledge to figure out.

comments.author: RigoJMortis
comments.body: I would recommend creating a new project, and give the AI the absolute bare minimum starting point to create this function. Have it create this part as if it were the whole game. However, make sure it knows that your pathing function needs to be reusable in other contexts (don't go into detail), and as such, able to be exported as a single unit.

replies.author: MosesSecondofHisName
replies.body: This is a good idea. I think I'll try this.

replies.author: RigoJMortis
replies.body: Curious how it goes for you!

comments.author: Fun_Document4477
comments.body: Step through your code in the debugger and figure out what’s actually happening. Generate some output(i.e. the current state or relevant information such as position, etc.) as it runs and go from there. If you’re just feeding prompts to an ai you will inevitably get broken code that will need to be debugged. If you can’t debug you should probably learn how to do that.

replies.author: MosesSecondofHisName
replies.body: I've been debugging (admittedly, this is all new to me, so I'm probably doing it wrong), which is where the new problems are coming from. I've been running things in console, but nothing has quite worked 100%. So I do something that seems like it should be the for sure fix, logically, and it ends up creating a new issue and not fixing the old one.

comments.author: nuker0S
comments.body:
In what environment do you develop your game? Unity? Unreal? 3D? 2D? How does the cave look? Is it procedurally generated?

And to recap, you want the enemy to wander a bit, and then go straight to the target?

Or you just want enemies to take different paths instead of one?

Or do you want the enemy to randomly search the cave(like a human would) while retaining knowledge to not search already searched corridors?

replies.author: MosesSecondofHisName
replies.body:
Right now, I'm just building it in Github. I'm new to all this, so I wanted to see what's possible before committing too hard, though the plan would be to move it to Unity if it works. It's 2D. The cave is basically a static grid. The player can add walls to it, though (though not while enemies are moving).

I want the last behavior you mentioned--enemies search the cave like a human would while remembering where they've been. I've made a memory system, but it's hard to tell if it's working because the enemies are behaving so unreliably. Even when I get them to not go straight to the target, they end up wandering for a bit before freezing, with no real logic that I can discern.

replies.author: nuker0S
replies.body:
Yeaaahhh... I meant a framework(language, libraries, target platform). Copilot is just an LLM that operates on files in the repository. I'm going to assume that's it's just Javascript and friends kinda deal.

I also guess that you are making a top-down tower defense, something like [dungeon warfare](https://store.steampowered.com/app/355980/Dungeon_Warfare/).

Pretty hard task i would say, especially because terrain isn't "hard coded" and algorithms that don't see the whole ass grid are pretty unpopular... Usually task like this are solved using Machine Learning.

In your place, i would first search for an algorithm and then tell AI to use it.

[https://arxiv.org/pdf/1806.03581](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1806.03581) [https://cdn.aaai.org/AAAI/2002/AAAI02-072.pdf](https://cdn.aaai.org/AAAI/2002/AAAI02-072.pdf) [https://idm-lab.org/bib/abstracts/papers/aamas06.pdf](https://idm-lab.org/bib/abstracts/papers/aamas06.pdf)

comments.author: kytheon
comments.body:
If you buy a finished asset, you'll never learn.
Figure out what's wrong and move from there. Also figure out exactly what the AI should know about the world, and what its goals are, and if multiple AIs can communicate. For example if one enemy finds the target, do the others know?

Why do they freeze? Did they try to search in an area that doesn't exist? It would help if you make the AIs give you feedback. Like "I'm searching sector A because..." and "I assume the target is nearby" etc. Freezing is probably just a mistake in your logic.
